claims.text: The starting material is as-received Q235 mild steel without prior mechanical or chemical modification.
Controlled high-temperature annealing in air can pre-form a thin, dense, and uniform oxide scale on Q235 steel.
The pre-formed scale on annealed Q235 will consist primarily of magnetite and/or hematite.
A compact oxide layer can act as a diffusion barrier to oxygen and hinder further oxidation.
The proposed Q235 oxide scale will retard penetration of sulfate/chloride salt species at 700–900 °C.
Retarding oxygen and salt transport through the oxide scale will reduce high-temperature corrosion degradation of Q235.
At room temperature, the oxide layer will be less fully coalesced because of slower kinetics.
Discontinuities in the room-temperature oxide layer will cause localized breakdown and pitting.
Oxide composition, thickness, porosity, adhesion, and continuity govern the scale's protective performance.
Relative to unannealed Q235, pre-oxidized Q235 will exhibit a lower mass change during exposure to 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl at 900 °C.
Relative to unannealed Q235, pre-oxidized Q235 will exhibit reduced pit formation during high-temperature salt exposure.
Relative to unannealed Q235, pre-oxidized Q235 will exhibit improved overall corrosion resistance during high-temperature salt exposure.
At room temperature, the protection provided by pre-oxidation will be less pronounced than at high temperature.
Unannealed Q235 will naturally form a non-uniform oxide during exposure and consequently experience greater degradation.
Oxide-scale sintering and self-healing are active on Q235 in aggressive salt environments at 700–900 °C.
At substantially lower annealing temperatures, oxide formation may be insufficient for the proposed protection.
The proposed protection may fail in environments that do not promote formation or stability of a protective oxide scale.

contradictions.description: The annealing intervention is said to create a dense, uniform scale before either exposure, yet the room-temperature branch says that the same pre-formed scale is less fully coalesced because room-temperature kinetics are slower. Exposure temperature cannot by itself explain deficient initial coalescence of a scale already formed during the common 700 °C anneal.
